MKT-01.Product: The good or service a business offers, including its features, quality, brand and packaging.
MKT-01.Price: What the customer pays for the product. The business must set it high enough to earn a profit and low enough that people will still buy.
MKT-01.Promotion: The ways a business tells customers about its product and persuades them to buy, such as advertising, selling and public relations.
MKT-01.Place: Where and how the product reaches the customer, covering the stores, websites and distribution channels used to get it there.
MKT-01.People: The employees who deliver a service and deal with customers. In services marketing their skill and attitude are part of what the customer is buying.
MKT-01.Packaging: The container and design that hold and present a product. Some newer lists add it as an extra P because the package helps sell the item.
MKT-01.Process: The steps a customer goes through to receive a service, such as ordering, waiting and paying. One of the three Ps added for services.
MKT-01.Positioning: The image a product holds in customers' minds compared with rival products. Some expanded versions of the mix list it as an extra P.
MKT-01.Physical evidence: The things a customer can see and touch that hint at a service's quality, such as the building, decor, uniforms and website.

MKT-02.Demographic: Dividing a market by measurable facts about people, such as age, gender, income, education and family size.
MKT-02.Geographic: Dividing a market by where customers live or work, such as country, region, city size or climate.
MKT-02.Psychographic: Dividing a market by lifestyle, personality, values and interests, so it groups people by how they think and live.
MKT-02.Behavioral: Dividing a market by how customers act toward a product, such as how often they buy, how loyal they are and what benefits they want.
MKT-02.Generational: Grouping customers by the era they were born in, such as Gen Z or baby boomers, because people who grew up together often share habits and tastes.
MKT-02.Usage rate: Grouping customers by how much of a product they use, such as heavy, medium and light users. A form of behavioral segmentation.
MKT-02.Benefits sought: Grouping customers by the main benefit they want from a product, such as low price, convenience or whiter teeth from a toothpaste.
MKT-02.Brand loyalty: Grouping customers by how faithful they are to a brand, from buyers who always choose it to those who switch freely.
MKT-02.Occasion: Grouping customers by when they buy or use a product, such as holidays, birthdays or a morning commute.
MKT-02.Technographic: Grouping customers by the technology they own and how they use it, such as their devices, apps and comfort with new tools.
MKT-02.Firmographic: Dividing business customers by facts about their organization, such as industry, number of employees, revenue and location.
MKT-02.Geodemographic: Combining where people live with demographic facts about them, on the idea that people in the same neighborhood tend to be alike.

MKT-03.Advertising: Paid, non-personal messages from an identified sponsor, carried by media such as television, websites, radio and print.
MKT-03.Social media: Posts, videos and paid messages on platforms such as Instagram and TikTok, where a business can talk with customers directly.
MKT-03.Public relations: Activities that build a good public image and earn unpaid media coverage, such as press releases and community events.
MKT-03.Sales promotion: Short-term incentives that encourage people to buy now, such as coupons, contests, rebates and free samples.
MKT-03.Personal selling: Direct, person-to-person communication in which a salesperson helps a customer and tries to make a sale.
MKT-03.Direct marketing: Messages sent straight to chosen individuals, by mail, email, phone or catalog, asking them to respond or order directly.
MKT-03.Influencer marketing: Paying or partnering with people who have a large online following so they show or recommend the product to their audience.
MKT-03.Word of mouth: Customers telling other people about a product. It is trusted because it comes from friends, not the seller, though the business cannot fully control it.
MKT-03.Event marketing: Promoting a brand by creating or taking part in events where customers can experience the product in person.
MKT-03.Visual merchandising: Using store displays, windows and layout to show products attractively and encourage shoppers to buy.
MKT-03.Sponsorship: Paying to support an event, team, person or cause in return for having the brand name linked with it and seen by its audience.
MKT-03.Product placement: Paying to have a branded product appear or be used within a film, show, video or game, so viewers see it as part of the story.

MKT-04.Discount pricing: Temporarily cutting the regular price to boost sales, clear stock or draw shoppers in.
MKT-04.Economy pricing: Keeping prices low all the time by holding production and marketing costs to a minimum, as with no-frills or budget products.
MKT-04.Premium pricing: Keeping the price high on purpose to signal high quality and appeal to buyers who will pay more for the best.
MKT-04.Competitive pricing: Setting a price mainly by looking at what rivals charge, then pricing at, just above or just below their level.
MKT-04.Bundle pricing: Selling several products together for one price that is lower than buying each item separately.
MKT-04.Penetration pricing: Launching a new product at a low price to win customers and market share quickly, often raising the price later.
MKT-04.Price skimming: Launching a new product at a high price to earn the most from eager early buyers, then lowering the price over time.
MKT-04.Dynamic pricing: Changing the price frequently as demand changes, as airlines and ride-share apps do at busy times.
MKT-04.Value-based pricing: Setting the price according to what customers believe the product is worth to them, not according to what it cost to make.
MKT-04.Psychological pricing: Choosing prices for the feeling they create in the buyer's mind, such as $9.99 seeming much cheaper than $10.
MKT-04.Cost-plus pricing: Working out what a product costs and then adding a set amount or percentage, the markup, to reach the selling price.
MKT-04.Freemium: Giving a basic version of a product away for free and charging for extra features or a full version. Common with apps and software.
MKT-04.Everyday low pricing: Charging steady low prices all the time, with few or no special sales, so shoppers trust they are always getting a fair deal.
MKT-04.Subscription pricing: Charging a regular fee, such as monthly or yearly, for ongoing access to a product or service.
MKT-04.Demand-based pricing: Setting the price by how much customers want the product, charging more when demand is strong and less when it is weak.
MKT-04.Loss leader: An item sold at or below its cost to pull shoppers into the store, in the hope they also buy other goods at full price.
MKT-04.Prestige pricing: Setting a high price to give a product an image of luxury and status. A lower price could actually make it less attractive.
MKT-04.Price lining: Selling the goods in a product line at a few set price points, such as $25, $40 and $60, so shoppers can compare levels easily.
MKT-04.High-low pricing: Charging a higher regular price and then running frequent sales with deep discounts on selected items.
MKT-04.Geographic pricing: Charging different prices in different places, often because shipping costs, taxes or local competition differ.
MKT-04.Multiple-unit pricing: Offering a lower price per item when several are bought together, such as three for $5.
MKT-04.Target return pricing: Setting the price so that expected sales will earn a chosen profit or a chosen percentage return on the money invested.
MKT-04.Segmented pricing: Selling the same product at different prices to different groups, times or places, such as cheaper movie tickets for children.
MKT-04.Odd-even pricing: Using odd prices such as $19.99 to suggest a bargain and even prices such as $20 or $200 to suggest quality.
MKT-04.Captive product pricing: Pricing a main product low and earning the profit on the supplies it needs, such as a cheap printer that uses costly ink.
MKT-04.Optional product pricing: Keeping the base product's price low and charging extra for add-ons the buyer may choose, such as upgrades on a new car.
MKT-04.Two-part pricing: Charging a fixed fee plus a separate charge for each use, such as a park entry fee plus a price per ride.
MKT-04.Flexible pricing: Letting the price be negotiated, so different customers may pay different amounts for the same item, as with cars.
MKT-04.Pay what you want: Letting each buyer choose the amount to pay, sometimes above a minimum. It relies on customers' sense of fairness.

MKT-05.Growth: The stage after introduction, when sales climb quickly, profits rise and competitors begin to enter the market.
MKT-05.Introduction: The stage when the product is launched onto the market. Sales are low and promotion costs are high, so profits are small or negative.
MKT-05.Maturity: The stage when sales level off at their peak. Most likely buyers already own the product and competition is at its strongest.
MKT-05.Decline: The final stage, when sales and profits fall as tastes change or newer products replace the old one.
MKT-05.Saturation: A point some models add late in maturity, when almost everyone who wants the product has it and sales can no longer grow.
MKT-05.Development: The stage before launch, when the idea is researched, designed and tested. The business spends money but has no sales yet.

MKT-06.Retailer: A business that sells goods directly to the final consumer, in a store or online. Usually the last intermediary in the channel.
MKT-06.Wholesaler: A business that buys goods in large quantities from producers and resells them to retailers or other businesses, not to the public.
MKT-06.Manufacturer: The business that makes the product, turning raw materials into finished goods. It is where the channel begins.
MKT-06.Consumer: The person who buys the product for personal use. The consumer is the final member, at the end of the channel.
MKT-06.Distributor: An intermediary that buys from producers and resells to businesses or retailers, often with rights to carry a brand in an area.
MKT-06.Intermediary: Any business that operates between the producer and the final buyer, such as a wholesaler, agent or retailer. Also called a middleman.
MKT-06.Agent: An intermediary that brings buyers and sellers together and earns a commission, without ever owning the goods being sold.
MKT-06.Supplier: A business that provides the raw materials, parts or goods another business needs in order to make or sell its own products.
MKT-06.Freight forwarder: A firm that arranges shipments for other businesses, combining small loads and booking carriers. It moves the goods but does not own them.
MKT-06.Industrial user: A business that buys products to use in its own operations or to make other goods, not to resell them as they are.
MKT-06.Importer: A business that buys goods from another country and brings them in to sell at home. An exporter does the reverse, selling home goods abroad.
MKT-06.Drop shipper: A wholesaler that takes orders and owns the goods but never handles them, having the producer ship straight to the customer.
MKT-06.Rack jobber: A wholesaler that sets up, stocks and manages its own display racks inside retail stores, often billing only for what sells.
MKT-06.Franchisee: A person or business that pays for the right to sell a franchisor's products under its brand name and operating system.
MKT-06.Value-added reseller: A business that buys a product, adds something such as software, installation or support, and resells the improved package.

MKT-07.Family: A social factor. Parents, partners and children shape what a person buys, and family members often make purchase decisions together.
MKT-07.Income: A personal factor. How much money a person has to spend limits what they can afford and which brands they consider.
MKT-07.Culture: The shared values, customs and beliefs a person learns from their society. It is the broadest influence on what people want and buy.
MKT-07.Age: A personal factor. Needs and tastes change as people grow older and move through life stages such as student, parent and retiree.
MKT-07.Reference groups: Groups a person belongs to or looks up to, such as friends, classmates and coworkers, whose opinions guide what that person buys.
MKT-07.Lifestyle: A personal factor describing how someone lives, shown by their activities, interests and opinions.
MKT-07.Personality: A personal factor. A person's lasting traits, such as being outgoing or cautious, lead them toward brands that fit how they see themselves.
MKT-07.Motivation: A psychological factor. The need or want that is strong enough to push a person to act, such as hunger, safety or a wish to belong.
MKT-07.Gender: A personal factor. Some products and marketing messages are aimed mainly at men or at women, and buying habits can differ between them.
MKT-07.Social media: A social factor. Posts, reviews and online communities expose people to products and to the opinions of other buyers.
MKT-07.Social class: A cultural factor. A group in society with similar income, education and occupation, whose members tend to buy in similar ways.
MKT-07.Perception: A psychological factor. The way a person notices and interprets information, so two people can view the same product very differently.
MKT-07.Attitudes: A psychological factor. A person's lasting likes or dislikes toward a product, brand or idea, which are hard to change.
MKT-07.Emotions: A psychological factor. Feelings such as excitement, fear or a passing mood can trigger a purchase, including impulse buys.
MKT-07.Education: A personal factor. A person's level of schooling affects their income and interests and how they research and judge products.
MKT-07.Occupation: A personal factor. A person's job affects what they need to buy, such as work clothes or tools, and how much they can spend.
MKT-07.Learning: A psychological factor. Changes in behavior that come from experience, so a good or bad past purchase shapes the next one.
MKT-07.Beliefs: A psychological factor. Ideas a person holds to be true about a product or brand, whether or not they are accurate.
MKT-07.Social roles: A social factor. The positions a person holds in groups, such as parent, manager or team captain, each with expected behavior and status.
MKT-07.Word of mouth: A social factor. Recommendations and warnings passed along by friends, family and other customers, which people trust more than ads.
MKT-07.Subculture: A cultural factor. A smaller group within a culture that shares its own values, such as a religious, ethnic or regional group.
MKT-07.Opinion leaders: A social factor. People whose knowledge or status makes others in a group copy their choices, such as experts or celebrities.

MKT-08.SWOT analysis: A review of the business's internal strengths and weaknesses and the external opportunities and threats it faces.
MKT-08.Target market: The section describing the specific group of customers the business will aim its marketing at, and what they are like.
MKT-08.Executive summary: A short overview at the start of the plan that sums up its main goals and recommendations for busy readers.
MKT-08.Situation analysis: A study of where the business stands now, covering its market, customers, competitors and outside conditions.
MKT-08.Marketing objectives: The specific, measurable results the plan aims for, such as raising sales by 10 percent within a year.
MKT-08.Budget: The section showing how much money the marketing activities will cost and how the spending is divided among them.
MKT-08.Marketing strategies: The broad approach the business will take to reach its objectives, including which market it targets and how it positions the product.
MKT-08.Marketing mix: The section setting out decisions on the four Ps: the product, its price, where it is sold and how it is promoted.
MKT-08.Competitive analysis: A study of rival businesses, their products, prices, strengths and weaknesses, to see how the business can compete.
MKT-08.Action plan: The section listing the specific tasks to be done, who is responsible for each and when it will happen.
MKT-08.Mission statement: A brief statement of the business's purpose, saying what it does and whom it serves. It guides the rest of the plan.
MKT-08.Company description: Background on the business itself, such as its history, what it sells, how it is organized and where it operates.
MKT-08.Market research: The section presenting the data gathered about customers and the market that supports the plan's decisions.
MKT-08.Evaluation and control: The section explaining how results will be measured against the objectives and what will be done if they fall short.
MKT-08.Timeline: A schedule showing when each marketing activity starts and finishes, so the work is done in order and on time.
MKT-08.Positioning statement: A sentence or two describing how the business wants its target customers to see the product compared with competing ones.
MKT-08.Unique selling proposition: The one feature or benefit that makes the product different from and better than its rivals, and the reason to choose it.
MKT-08.Sales forecast: An estimate of how many units or dollars the business expects to sell over a future period.
MKT-08.Appendix: The final section holding supporting material, such as research data, charts and detailed tables, that would clutter the main plan.
MKT-08.Contingency plan: A backup plan describing what the business will do if things go wrong, such as weak sales or a new competitor.

MKT-09.Convenience products: Low-priced items people buy often and with little effort or comparison, such as bread, snacks and toothpaste.
MKT-09.Consumer products: Goods and services bought by final consumers for personal or household use. One of the two broad product classes.
MKT-09.Shopping products: Items people buy less often and compare on price, quality and style before choosing, such as clothing, furniture and phones.
MKT-09.Specialty products: Items with unique features or a brand that buyers insist on and will make a special effort to get, such as a luxury watch.
MKT-09.Impulse goods: Convenience products bought on the spot without planning, such as candy and magazines placed beside the checkout.
MKT-09.Business products: Goods and services bought by organizations to use in making other products or in running the business. Also called industrial goods.
MKT-09.Unsought products: Products people do not know about or do not normally think of buying, such as life insurance or funeral services.
MKT-09.Staple goods: Convenience products bought regularly and routinely, such as milk, bread and soap.
MKT-09.Raw materials: Business products in their natural state that become part of a finished good, such as crude oil, timber, cotton and wheat.
MKT-09.Durable goods: Products that last through many uses over a long time, usually three years or more, such as cars, appliances and furniture.
MKT-09.Emergency goods: Convenience products bought when an urgent need arises, such as an umbrella in a storm or bandages after a cut.
MKT-09.Supplies: Business products used up in running a company that do not become part of what it makes, such as paper, cleaning products and light bulbs.
MKT-09.Component parts: Finished items a business buys and builds into its own product without changing them, such as tires on a car.
MKT-09.Nondurable goods: Products used up quickly, in one or a few uses, such as food, shampoo and gasoline.
MKT-09.Installations: Major, long-lasting business purchases such as buildings and heavy machinery. They cost a lot and are bought rarely.
MKT-09.Accessory equipment: Smaller, shorter-lived equipment that helps a business operate but is not part of the finished product, such as computers and hand tools.
MKT-09.Business services: Work one business pays another to do for it, such as cleaning, repairs, accounting or legal advice.
MKT-09.Processed materials: Business products that have already been partly manufactured and need more processing before use, such as steel, lumber and flour.

MKT-11.Age: How old customers are. Needs and tastes change with age, so marketers often aim products at children, teens, adults or seniors.
MKT-11.Gender: Whether customers are male or female. Products such as clothing, cosmetics and grooming items are often marketed by gender.
MKT-11.Income: How much money a person or household earns. It tells marketers who can afford budget, mid-priced or luxury products.
MKT-11.Education: The highest level of schooling a person has completed, which is linked to income, interests and media habits.
MKT-11.Occupation: The kind of work a person does, such as student, tradesperson or professional, which shapes their needs and spending.
MKT-11.Ethnicity: A person's racial or cultural background. Groups may differ in tastes, traditions and the media they use.
MKT-11.Marital status: Whether a person is single, married, divorced or widowed. It affects spending on housing, travel, insurance and more.
MKT-11.Family size: The number of people in a household, which affects how much food, space and transportation the household buys.
MKT-11.Religion: A person's faith, which can guide choices about food, clothing, holidays and other purchases.
MKT-11.Generation: A group of people born in the same period, such as Gen Z or millennials, who shared similar experiences while growing up.
MKT-11.Family life cycle: The stage a household has reached, such as single, married with young children or empty nest. Each stage has different needs.
MKT-11.Nationality: The country a person comes from or is a citizen of, which can shape their tastes, traditions and brand choices.
MKT-11.Home ownership: Whether a household owns or rents its home. Owners are better targets for goods such as lawn mowers, renovations and home insurance.
MKT-11.Language: The main language a person speaks, which tells a marketer what language to use in ads, packaging and customer service.

SEL-01.Closing the sale: The step where the salesperson asks for the order and gets the customer's agreement to buy.
SEL-01.Presentation: The step where the salesperson shows the product and explains how its features and benefits meet the customer's needs.
SEL-01.Prospecting: The first step: searching for potential customers, called prospects or leads, who might need the product.
SEL-01.Approach: The first face-to-face contact with the customer, when the salesperson greets them and tries to make a good first impression.
SEL-01.Determining needs: Asking questions and listening to find out what the customer wants, so the right product can be recommended.
SEL-01.Handling objections: Answering the customer's doubts or reasons for not buying, such as price, in a helpful and honest way.
SEL-01.Follow-up: Contacting the customer after the sale to check they are satisfied, solve any problems and build a relationship for future sales.
SEL-01.Suggestion selling: Recommending extra or related items that go with the purchase, such as a case for a new phone.
SEL-01.Qualifying: Checking whether a prospect has the need, the money and the authority to buy, so time is not wasted on unlikely buyers.
SEL-01.Negotiation: Working out terms such as price, delivery and payment that both the buyer and the seller can accept. Common in business sales.
SEL-01.Preapproach: The preparation done before meeting a prospect, such as researching the customer and planning what to say.

SEL-02.Direct close: Simply asking the customer for the order in plain words, such as asking whether they would like to buy it today.
SEL-02.Assumptive close: Acting as though the customer has already decided to buy, for example by asking where the item should be delivered.
SEL-02.Urgency close: Giving the customer a real reason to decide now, such as a sale that ends today or a price that is about to rise.
SEL-02.Summary close: Repeating the main benefits the customer liked during the presentation, then asking for the order.
SEL-02.Alternative choice close: Offering a choice between two options, both of which mean a sale, such as asking whether they prefer the red or the blue.
SEL-02.Special offer close: Adding an extra incentive, such as a discount, free delivery or a bonus item, to win the customer's decision.
SEL-02.Trial close: A question asked during the presentation to test how ready the customer is to buy, such as asking how the product feels so far.
SEL-02.Takeaway close: Suggesting the product or part of the offer may not be right for or available to the customer, which can make them want it more.
SEL-02.Puppy dog close: Letting the customer take the product home and try it with no commitment, expecting they will not want to give it back.
SEL-02.Standing room only close: Pointing out that supply is limited or that others want the item, so the customer should buy before it is gone. It must be true to be ethical.
SEL-02.Service close: Offering services that remove a barrier to buying, such as free installation, delivery, a warranty or a payment plan.
SEL-02.Ben Franklin close: Listing the reasons for and against buying in two columns, so the customer can see that the reasons to buy outweigh the rest.
SEL-02.Sharp angle close: Answering a customer's request for a concession by agreeing to it only if they commit to buying right away.
SEL-02.Minor points close: Getting agreement on small details, such as color or delivery date, which leads the customer toward the bigger decision to buy.
SEL-02.Testimonial close: Sharing the story or praise of a satisfied customer in a similar situation to give the buyer confidence to go ahead.

SEL-03.Price: The customer feels the product costs too much or says they cannot afford it. The most common objection.
SEL-03.Need: The customer does not believe they need the product, or is content with what they already have.
SEL-03.Time: The customer is not ready to decide yet and wants to wait or think it over. It often hides another concern.
SEL-03.Product: The customer has a concern about the item itself, such as its quality, size, color, style or features.
SEL-03.Competitor: The customer already buys from, or prefers, a rival brand or supplier and sees no reason to switch.
SEL-03.Authority: The person says they cannot make the decision alone and must first ask someone else, such as a boss or spouse.
SEL-03.Source: The customer has doubts about the company, the brand, the store or the salesperson, not about the product itself.
SEL-03.Hidden objection: A real reason for not buying that the customer keeps to themselves, often while giving a different excuse.

SEL-04.Demonstration: Answering the objection by showing the product in action, so the customer sees for themselves that the concern is unfounded.
SEL-04.Question method: Asking the customer questions about the objection to learn more about it and help them rethink it themselves.
SEL-04.Third-party method: Using the words or experience of a neutral outsider, such as a satisfied customer's testimonial, to answer the concern.
SEL-04.Substitution: Recommending a different product that better meets the customer's needs when the first one does not suit them.
SEL-04.Denial: Politely but directly telling the customer that their objection is based on wrong information, and giving proof of the facts.
SEL-04.Yes-but method: Agreeing that the customer's concern is reasonable, then offering another point of view that offsets it.
SEL-04.Feel felt found: Saying you understand how the customer feels, that others felt the same way, and what those others found after buying.
SEL-04.Boomerang: Turning the objection back into a reason to buy, for example by explaining that the high price reflects longer-lasting quality.
SEL-04.Trial offer: Letting the customer try the product, or backing it with a money-back guarantee, to remove the risk they are worried about.
SEL-04.Superior-point method: Admitting the objection is valid, then pointing to a stronger feature or benefit that outweighs it.
SEL-04.Forestalling: Raising and answering a likely objection yourself during the presentation, before the customer has a chance to bring it up.

SEL-05.Referrals: Names of possible buyers given by satisfied customers. In the endless chain method the salesperson asks every customer for more names.
SEL-05.Cold calling: Contacting people by phone or in person with no earlier contact and no sign that they are interested.
SEL-05.Networking: Meeting and staying in touch with people at business and social events so that contacts can lead to prospects.
SEL-05.Social media: Using platforms such as LinkedIn or Instagram to find people who fit the customer profile and to start conversations with them.
SEL-05.Friends and family: Starting with people the salesperson already knows, who may buy or may introduce other buyers. Common for new salespeople.
SEL-05.Email: Sending messages to people or businesses that might need the product, hoping some will reply and show interest.
SEL-05.Trade shows: Events where businesses in an industry display their products, giving salespeople the chance to meet many interested buyers at once.
SEL-05.Current customers: People who have bought before. Company records show who may be ready to buy again, upgrade or try another product.
SEL-05.Internet research: Searching online for businesses or people who match the ideal customer, using search engines and company websites.
SEL-05.Directories: Published lists of people or businesses, such as phone books and industry directories, used to look up names and contact details.
SEL-05.Company leads: Names passed to the salesperson by their own employer, gathered from website forms, inquiries and marketing campaigns.
SEL-05.Advertising: Ads that invite people to call, click or send for information. Those who respond have shown interest and become leads.
SEL-05.Direct mail: Letters, postcards or brochures sent to a list of likely buyers, inviting those who are interested to respond.
SEL-05.Organizations and clubs: Groups such as a chamber of commerce, trade association or civic club, where a salesperson can meet members who may become customers.
SEL-05.Commercial lists: Lists of names and contact details bought from companies that collect them, usually sorted by features such as income or industry.
SEL-05.Newspapers: News stories and announcements, such as new businesses, promotions, weddings and births, that point to people with new needs.
SEL-05.Seminars: Free talks or online webinars on a useful topic. The people who attend are interested in the subject and so are likely prospects.
SEL-05.Public records: Government files open to anyone, such as building permits and business licenses, which reveal people likely to need certain products.
SEL-05.Center of influence: A well-known, well-connected person, such as a banker or club leader, who can introduce the salesperson to likely buyers.
SEL-05.Spotters: People who come across likely buyers in their daily work and pass the names to the salesperson, sometimes for a fee. Also called bird dogs.

SEL-06.Loyalty program: A plan that rewards repeat buying with points, free items or perks, giving customers a reason to keep choosing the same business.
SEL-06.Customer service: The help and care given to customers before, during and after a purchase. Friendly, reliable service makes people want to return.
SEL-06.Follow-up call: Contacting the customer shortly after the sale to check that they are happy with the purchase and to fix any problem early.
SEL-06.Thank-you note: A short message of appreciation sent after a purchase. It makes the customer feel valued and keeps the business in mind.
SEL-06.Quality products: Goods that work well and last. A product that lives up to its promise is the most basic reason a customer buys again.
SEL-06.Exclusive discounts: Special prices or coupons offered only to existing customers or members, rewarding them for coming back.
SEL-06.Satisfaction survey: A short set of questions asking customers how their experience was. It shows the business cares and reveals what to improve.
SEL-06.Warranty: A written promise to repair or replace a product that fails within a set time. It builds trust in the business.
SEL-06.Newsletter: Regular emails or mailings with news, tips and offers that keep customers in touch with the business between purchases.
SEL-06.Easy returns: A simple, fair policy for sending back or exchanging purchases. It lowers the risk of buying, so customers feel safe shopping there again.
SEL-06.Complaint resolution: Dealing with a customer's problem quickly and fairly. A complaint that is handled well can turn an unhappy buyer into a loyal one.
SEL-06.Personalized offers: Deals and recommendations chosen for one customer based on what they bought or looked at before.
SEL-06.After-sale service: Help provided once the product is bought, such as delivery, installation, repairs, maintenance and technical support.
SEL-06.Social media engagement: Replying to comments, answering questions and sharing content online, so customers feel connected to the brand.
SEL-06.Free gifts: Small extras or samples given to customers at no charge, which create goodwill and may introduce them to other products.
SEL-06.Referral program: A reward, such as a discount or credit, given to existing customers who bring in a new customer.
SEL-06.Customer training: Classes, tutorials or guides that teach buyers how to use the product well, so they get more value from it and stay satisfied.
SEL-06.Birthday rewards: A discount, free item or greeting sent for a customer's birthday, a personal touch that prompts another visit.
SEL-06.Subscription program: An arrangement in which customers pay regularly to receive a product or service automatically, which locks in repeat sales.
SEL-06.Mobile app: A phone application that lets customers order, collect rewards and receive offers easily, keeping the business close at hand.
SEL-06.Customer appreciation event: A special sale, party or preview held to thank existing customers and make them feel like valued insiders.
SEL-06.Reorder reminders: Messages telling customers it is time to buy again or book a service, such as a refill, an oil change or a check-up.

SEL-07.Retail salesperson: Someone who sells goods to shoppers in a store, helping them find products, answering questions and completing the purchase.
SEL-07.Telemarketer: A salesperson who sells products or sets up appointments by telephone instead of meeting customers in person.
SEL-07.Business-to-business sales: Selling goods and services to other companies instead of to consumers. Orders are larger and the buying process is usually longer.
SEL-07.Real estate agent: A licensed salesperson who helps people buy, sell or rent property and is usually paid a commission on each deal.
SEL-07.Car salesperson: Someone who sells new or used vehicles at a dealership, often negotiating the price and usually earning commission.
SEL-07.Sales manager: The person who leads a sales team by hiring, training and motivating salespeople and setting their sales targets.
SEL-07.Inside sales: Selling from the company's own office by phone, email or video call, without traveling to visit customers.
SEL-07.Outside sales: Selling by traveling to meet customers face to face at their homes or places of business. Also called field sales.
SEL-07.Insurance agent: A licensed salesperson who sells insurance policies, such as car, home, health or life insurance, and helps clients choose coverage.
SEL-07.Order taker: A salesperson who mainly completes sales to customers who already want the product, such as a cashier or a clerk handling reorders.
SEL-07.Order getter: A salesperson who actively seeks out new customers and persuades them to buy, which takes more selling skill than taking orders.
SEL-07.Account manager: A salesperson responsible for looking after particular existing customers, keeping them satisfied and growing their business.
SEL-07.Direct seller: Someone who sells to consumers away from a store, such as door to door, at home parties or through personal contacts.
SEL-07.Pharmaceutical sales representative: A salesperson who visits doctors and pharmacists to explain a drug company's medicines so they will prescribe or stock them.
SEL-07.Wholesale salesperson: Someone who works for a wholesaler and sells goods in quantity to retailers and other businesses.
SEL-07.Manufacturers representative: An independent salesperson who sells the products of several manufacturers in a territory and is paid by commission.
SEL-07.Sales engineer: A salesperson with technical training who explains complex products and shows how they solve a customer's technical problem.
SEL-07.Sales support: Staff who help make sales happen without closing them, for example by giving technical advice or handling paperwork.
SEL-07.Sales development representative: A salesperson who finds and qualifies new leads, then passes the promising ones to a colleague who closes the sale.
SEL-07.Missionary salesperson: Someone who builds goodwill and educates buyers about a product without taking orders directly, such as a drug rep visiting doctors.
SEL-07.Trade salesperson: A salesperson who calls on wholesalers and retailers to keep them stocking and promoting the producer's goods.
SEL-07.Route salesperson: Someone who drives a regular route delivering goods such as bread or snacks to stores and selling to them on each stop.

SEL-08.Using the product: Trying the product personally. First-hand experience lets a salesperson describe honestly how it works and feels.
SEL-08.Company training: Classes and sessions run by the employer to teach salespeople about the products, their features and how to sell them.
SEL-08.Company website: The business's or manufacturer's own site, which lists product details, features, prices and answers to common questions.
SEL-08.Product labels: The label, tag or package on the item, which states facts such as contents, size, materials and care or use directions.
SEL-08.Owner manuals: The instruction booklets that come with a product, explaining how to set it up, use it, look after it and fix simple problems.
SEL-08.Coworkers: Experienced salespeople and managers who can share what they know about the products and what customers usually ask.
SEL-08.Advertisements: The company's own ads and promotional material, which show the features and benefits the business wants customers to notice.
SEL-08.Catalogs: Printed or online booklets and brochures that picture the product range and list descriptions, sizes, options and prices.
SEL-08.Customers: People who own the product. Their comments and reviews reveal how it performs in real use and what buyers like or dislike.
SEL-08.Manufacturer representatives: Salespeople from the company that makes or supplies the product, who visit to explain new items and answer technical questions.
SEL-08.Online videos: Product demonstrations, tutorials and recorded training on the web that show how an item works and how to use it.
SEL-08.Trade publications: Magazines and journals written for people in one industry, reporting on new products, trends and comparisons.
SEL-08.Warranties: The written guarantee with a product, which tells the salesperson what is covered, for how long and what the maker will repair.
SEL-08.Trade shows: Industry events where makers display and demonstrate their newest products, letting salespeople see them and ask questions.
SEL-08.Specification sheets: Documents listing a product's exact technical details, such as size, weight, materials, capacity and performance figures.
SEL-08.Sales meetings: Regular gatherings of the sales team where new products, features, promotions and selling tips are explained and discussed.
SEL-08.Competitor products: Rival goods, studied so the salesperson knows how their own product differs and can compare the two honestly.
SEL-08.Product testing reports: Results from independent groups that test and rate products, such as consumer magazines, giving an unbiased view of quality.
SEL-08.Factory tours: Visits to the place where the product is made, showing the salesperson the materials and care that go into it.

PROM-01.Television: A broadcast medium that combines sight, sound and motion to reach very large audiences. Air time and production are expensive.
PROM-01.Social media: Platforms such as Instagram, Facebook and TikTok, where ads appear among users' posts and can be aimed at very specific groups.
PROM-01.Internet: Online advertising such as banner ads, pop-ups and video ads on websites, which can be targeted and tracked click by click.
PROM-01.Radio: An audio-only broadcast medium. Ads are fairly cheap, can target a local area or a station's type of listener, and reach people in cars.
PROM-01.Newspaper: A print medium read daily or weekly, good for timely local ads such as store sales. Ads have a short life.
PROM-01.Magazine: A print medium aimed at readers with a shared interest. It offers high-quality color and a long life, but ads must be booked well ahead.
PROM-01.Billboard: A large outdoor sign beside a road or on a building, seen again and again by passing traffic. The message must be very short.
PROM-01.Search engine: Paid listings that appear beside search results when someone types in related words, so the ad reaches people already looking.
PROM-01.Direct mail: Advertising sent through the mail to chosen homes or businesses, such as letters, postcards, flyers and catalogs.
PROM-01.Email: Advertising messages and newsletters sent to the inboxes of people on a mailing list. It is cheap and easy to personalize.
PROM-01.Streaming services: Online video and music platforms that show or play ads to viewers, often chosen by what each household watches.
PROM-01.Posters: Printed sheets or flyers displayed in public places or handed out, a cheap way to advertise local events and offers.
PROM-01.Transit advertising: Ads placed on or inside buses, trains and taxis and at stops and stations, seen by commuters and people on the street.
PROM-01.Podcast: Audio shows people download or stream. Ads are often read aloud by the host, whom loyal listeners tend to trust.
PROM-01.Mobile advertising: Ads delivered to phones and tablets through apps, text messages and mobile websites, sometimes based on the user's location.
PROM-01.Directory: A printed or online listing of businesses by category, such as the Yellow Pages, used by people who are ready to buy.
PROM-01.Cinema: Ads shown on the big screen before a film starts, to an audience that is seated and paying attention.
PROM-01.In-store advertising: Signs, displays, screens and announcements inside a shop that reach customers at the moment they are deciding what to buy.
PROM-01.Specialty media: Useful, low-cost items printed with a business's name or logo and given away, such as pens, mugs, calendars and caps.
PROM-01.Aerial advertising: Messages shown in the sky, such as banners towed by planes, blimps and skywriting, usually over crowds at beaches or events.
PROM-01.Video games: Ads built into games, such as branded billboards in a racing game, or whole games made to promote a brand.

PROM-02.Coupons: Printed or digital certificates that give the holder a set saving on a product when they are presented at purchase.
PROM-02.Price deals: Temporary price cuts, such as a sale or cents-off offer, that give shoppers a reason to buy now.
PROM-02.Buy one get one: An offer where the shopper who buys one item gets a second free or at a reduced price. Often shortened to BOGO.
PROM-02.Free samples: Small amounts of a product given away so people can try it at no risk. Good for launching new products.
PROM-02.Contests: Promotions in which people compete for prizes by showing a skill, such as writing a slogan or submitting a photo.
PROM-02.Loyalty programs: Plans that reward repeat buyers with points, discounts or free items, encouraging them to keep coming back.
PROM-02.Sweepstakes: Prize draws in which winners are picked by chance. Entrants need luck, not skill, and usually need not buy anything.
PROM-02.Rebates: Part of the purchase price returned to the buyer after the sale, usually once proof of purchase is sent to the maker.
PROM-02.Free trial: Letting people use a product or service at no cost for a limited time, hoping they will pay to keep it afterward.
PROM-02.Premiums: Items given free or at low cost as a reward for buying a product, such as a toy in a cereal box.
PROM-02.Point-of-purchase displays: Special displays set up in stores, often near the checkout or at the end of aisles, to draw attention and prompt impulse buys.
PROM-02.Demonstrations: Showing a product in use, often in a store, so shoppers can see how it works or taste it before buying.
PROM-02.Free shipping: An offer to deliver an order at no charge, often for a limited time or above a minimum spend, to encourage online buying.
PROM-02.Product placement: Paying to have a brand appear in a film, show or game. Some textbooks list it under sales promotion, others treat it as advertising.
PROM-02.Trade shows: Industry exhibitions where producers display and demonstrate products to retailers and business buyers. A trade promotion tool.
PROM-02.Bonus packs: Packages that contain extra product at the regular price, such as 25 percent more free.
PROM-02.Promotional products: Useful items carrying the company's name or logo, such as pens, bags and shirts, given away to keep the brand in view.
PROM-02.Sponsorship: Paying to support an event, team or cause in exchange for brand exposure. Many textbooks class it under public relations instead.
PROM-02.Tie-in promotion: A joint promotion between two or more brands or businesses, such as a film character's toys offered with a fast-food meal.
PROM-02.Trade allowances: Discounts or payments a producer gives to retailers and wholesalers in return for stocking, displaying or promoting its product.
PROM-02.Push money: Cash bonuses a manufacturer pays to a retailer's salespeople for each unit of its product they sell. Also called spiffs.
PROM-02.Sales contests: Competitions that reward dealers or salespeople with prizes, such as cash or trips, for selling the most or beating a target.
PROM-02.Cooperative advertising: An arrangement in which a manufacturer pays part of a retailer's advertising cost when the ad features the manufacturer's product.

PROM-03.Press release: A short written announcement sent to the media in the hope that reporters will turn it into a news story.
PROM-03.Press conference: A meeting to which reporters are invited so a company can make an announcement and answer their questions.
PROM-03.Sponsorship: Paying to support an event, team or cause so the company's name is linked with something the public values.
PROM-03.Social media: Company accounts used to share news, respond to the public and shape the organization's image without buying ad space.
PROM-03.Community events: Local activities a business hosts or joins, such as fundraisers and volunteer days, which show it cares about the area.
PROM-03.Charitable donations: Gifts of money, goods or scholarships to good causes, which build goodwill and a caring reputation.
PROM-03.Media relations: Building working relationships with reporters and editors and offering them story ideas, so the company gets fair coverage.
PROM-03.Press kit: A package of materials for reporters, such as press releases, photos, fact sheets and background on the company.
PROM-03.Speeches: Talks given by company leaders at conferences, schools or community groups, presenting the organization and its views in person.
PROM-03.Newsletter: A regular publication sent to employees, customers or investors with news about the company, keeping those groups informed.
PROM-03.Media interview: A company spokesperson answering a reporter's questions for a news story, broadcast or podcast.
PROM-03.Company blog: Articles the company posts on its own website to share news, expertise and its side of a story directly with the public.
PROM-03.Annual report: A yearly document for shareholders and the public that reviews the company's finances and achievements.
PROM-03.Feature article: A longer, in-depth story about a company, its people or its product, written by or placed with a publication.
PROM-03.Crisis management: A planned response to bad news, such as a product recall or scandal, meant to protect the company's reputation.
PROM-03.Cause marketing: A partnership between a business and a charity or cause, such as donating part of each sale, which benefits both.
PROM-03.Public service announcement: A message in the public interest, such as a safety or health reminder, that media run free of charge.
PROM-03.Facility tours: Inviting the public, students or reporters to visit the company's premises to see how it works and build goodwill.
PROM-03.Lobbying: Communicating with lawmakers and government officials to influence laws and rules that affect the organization.
PROM-03.Video news release: A ready-made video story produced by a company and sent to television stations for use in their news programs.
PROM-03.Corporate identity materials: Items carrying the company's logo and look, such as stationery, brochures, signs and uniforms, that make it recognizable.

PROM-04.Impressions: The number of times an ad or post is displayed on a screen, whether or not anyone clicks. One person can count several times.
PROM-04.Followers: The number of people who have chosen to subscribe to a brand's social media account, a rough measure of audience size.
PROM-04.Website traffic: The number of visits a website receives in a period, showing how many people the marketing is bringing to the site.
PROM-04.Click-through rate: The percentage of people who saw an ad or link and clicked on it. Found by dividing clicks by impressions.
PROM-04.Conversion rate: The percentage of visitors who take the action the marketer wants, such as buying, signing up or downloading.
PROM-04.Reach: The number of different people who saw the content at least once. Unlike impressions, each person is counted only once.
PROM-04.Engagement rate: The share of an audience that interacts with a post through likes, comments, shares or saves.
PROM-04.Revenue: The total money from sales that a campaign or channel brought in, the most direct sign of whether it paid off.
PROM-04.Bounce rate: The percentage of visitors who leave a website after viewing only one page, without clicking anything else.
PROM-04.Cost per click: The average amount an advertiser pays each time someone clicks its ad. Total ad cost divided by number of clicks.
PROM-04.Return on investment: The profit a campaign earned compared with what it cost, usually shown as a percentage. Often shortened to ROI.
PROM-04.Cost per thousand: The cost of showing an ad one thousand times. Shortened to CPM, where M is the Roman numeral for a thousand.
PROM-04.Open rate: The percentage of people who received a marketing email and opened it.
PROM-04.Return on ad spend: The revenue earned for every dollar spent on advertising. Revenue from the ads divided by the cost of the ads.
PROM-04.Leads generated: The number of potential customers who showed interest by giving their contact details, such as by filling in a form.
PROM-04.App downloads: The number of times a company's mobile app has been installed, used to judge campaigns that promote the app.
PROM-04.Cost per acquisition: The average amount spent on marketing to get one desired action, such as a sale or sign-up. Shortened to CPA.
PROM-04.Customer acquisition cost: The total sales and marketing spending divided by the number of new customers gained in that period.
PROM-04.Search ranking: The position of a web page in a search engine's unpaid results for a given keyword. Higher positions get far more clicks.
PROM-04.Brand mentions: The number of times people name the brand online, in posts, comments, reviews or hashtags.
PROM-04.Average session duration: The average length of time a visitor spends on a website during one visit. Longer visits suggest more interest.
PROM-04.Unsubscribe rate: The percentage of email recipients who opt out of the mailing list after receiving a message.
PROM-04.Cart abandonment rate: The percentage of online shoppers who put items in a shopping cart but leave without completing the purchase.
PROM-04.Customer lifetime value: An estimate of the total money a customer will spend with a business over the whole time they remain a customer.

PROM-05.Window display: The arrangement of goods and props in a store's front windows, designed to catch the eye of passers-by and draw them in.
PROM-05.Signage: The signs, banners and posters in and around a store that name it, direct shoppers, and announce prices and offers.
PROM-05.Lighting: The lights used to make a store inviting and to highlight particular products, such as spotlights on a display.
PROM-05.Mannequins: Life-size model figures used to show how clothing and accessories look when they are worn.
PROM-05.Store layout: The plan for how floor space, aisles, fixtures and departments are arranged, which guides how shoppers move through the store.
PROM-05.Color: The colors used on walls, displays and signs, chosen to set a mood, attract attention and fit the store's image.
PROM-05.Store interior: The inside look of the store, including its walls, decor and furnishings, which shapes how shoppers feel while they browse.
PROM-05.Merchandise arrangement: The way products are grouped and placed on shelves and displays so they are easy to find and tempting to buy.
PROM-05.Fixtures: The permanent or movable furniture that holds and shows merchandise, such as shelves, racks, counters, tables and display cases.
PROM-05.Storefront: The outside of the store, including its sign, entrance, awning and windows, which gives shoppers their first impression.
PROM-05.Point-of-purchase display: A special display placed where buying decisions are made, such as beside the checkout, to prompt unplanned purchases.
PROM-05.Music: The background sound played in a store, chosen to suit the customers and affect their mood and how long they stay.
PROM-05.Props: Objects added to a display to set a scene or support a theme, such as beach chairs beside swimwear. They are not usually for sale.
PROM-05.End cap: The display at the end of a shelving aisle. It is highly visible, so retailers use it for featured, new or sale items.
PROM-05.Flooring: The floor covering, such as carpet, wood or tile, which affects a store's image and can mark out departments or pathways.
PROM-05.Display theme: A single idea, such as a season or holiday, that ties together the products, props and colors in a display.
PROM-05.Planogram: A diagram showing exactly where each product should be placed on the shelves or fixtures, so every store looks the same.
PROM-05.Atmospherics: The overall mood of a store created through the senses, including its lighting, music, scent and temperature.
PROM-05.Focal point: The spot in a display where the eye is meant to land first, usually holding the item the retailer most wants shoppers to notice.

PROM-06.Product advertising: Advertising that promotes a specific good or service and tries to persuade people to buy it.
PROM-06.Persuasive advertising: Advertising that tries to convince people one brand is better than others. Used heavily once competitors enter the market.
PROM-06.Informative advertising: Advertising that tells people about a product, such as what it does, what it costs and where to get it. Common for new products.
PROM-06.Comparative advertising: Advertising that directly or indirectly compares a brand with a named or recognizable competitor to show it is better.
PROM-06.Institutional advertising: Advertising that promotes the image and goodwill of a whole organization instead of selling one particular product.
PROM-06.Reminder advertising: Advertising that keeps an already well-known product in customers' minds, typical of the mature stage of a product's life.
PROM-06.Public service announcement: A non-commercial message that promotes a cause or public good, such as road safety. Media usually run it for free.
PROM-06.Political advertising: Advertising paid for by candidates, parties or interest groups to win votes or support for an issue.
PROM-06.National advertising: Advertising by a manufacturer or brand owner to audiences across the country, building demand for the brand wherever it is sold.
PROM-06.Consumer advertising: Advertising aimed at the people who will buy the product for their own personal or household use.
PROM-06.Cooperative advertising: Advertising whose cost is shared by a manufacturer and a retailer, with the ad featuring both the product and the local store.
PROM-06.Advocacy advertising: Advertising in which an organization states its position on a public issue and tries to win support for that view.
PROM-06.Retail advertising: Advertising by a local store telling nearby shoppers what it sells, its prices, sales, hours and location.
PROM-06.Business-to-business advertising: Advertising aimed at companies and professionals who buy products for their organizations, not for personal use.
PROM-06.Direct-response advertising: Advertising that asks the audience to act right away, such as by calling, clicking or ordering, so results can be measured.
PROM-06.Trade advertising: Advertising aimed at wholesalers and retailers to persuade them to stock and promote a producer's goods.
PROM-06.Pioneering advertising: Advertising that builds demand for a whole new type of product, not one brand. Used in the introduction stage.
PROM-06.Reinforcement advertising: Advertising that reassures people who have already bought the product that they made the right choice.
PROM-06.Corrective advertising: Advertising that a regulator such as the Federal Trade Commission orders a company to run to correct earlier false or misleading claims.
PROM-06.Recruitment advertising: Advertising an employer uses to attract job applicants, such as help-wanted ads and careers campaigns.

PROM-07.Headline: The large words, usually at the top of an ad, that grab attention and make people want to read on. Often the most-read part of an ad.
PROM-07.Illustration: The photograph or drawing in an ad. It attracts attention and shows the product, its use or the feeling it gives.
PROM-07.Copy: The main selling message of an ad in words. It expands on the headline, explains the benefits and gives reasons to buy.
PROM-07.Logo: The distinctive name or symbol that identifies the business. In a print ad it is also called the signature and tells who is selling.
PROM-07.Slogan: A short, memorable phrase that sums up the brand and is repeated across its ads. Also called a tagline.
PROM-07.Call to action: The words telling readers what to do next, such as visit the store, call today or order online.
PROM-07.Subheadline: A smaller line under the main headline that adds detail and leads the reader into the body copy.
PROM-07.Contact information: Details that tell readers how to reach or find the business, such as its address, phone number, website and opening hours.
PROM-07.Price: The amount the product costs, shown in the ad. Retail ads often feature it heavily, especially a sale price.
PROM-07.Border: A line or frame around the edge of an ad that separates it from other items on the page and holds its parts together.
PROM-07.Caption: A short line of text placed under or beside a picture to explain what it shows.
PROM-07.White space: The empty area of an ad with no words or pictures. It keeps the ad from looking crowded and draws the eye to what matters.
PROM-07.Coupon: A section of the ad readers can cut out or scan to get a discount. It gives a reason to act and helps measure the ad's response.
PROM-07.QR code: A square pattern (QR stands for quick response) that readers scan with a phone camera to open a web page or offer.
PROM-07.Disclaimer: The small print that states legal conditions and limits on an offer, such as expiration dates, exclusions or required warnings.

PRC-01.Costs: What the business spends to make, buy and sell the product. The price must cover these costs to earn a profit, so they set its floor.
PRC-01.Competition: What rival businesses charge for similar products. Customers compare, so a business cannot price far above rivals without a good reason.
PRC-01.Demand: How much of the product customers want and are able to buy. Strong demand lets a business charge more.
PRC-01.Supply: How much of the product is available for sale. When supply is short compared with demand, prices tend to rise.
PRC-01.Economic conditions: The state of the economy, such as inflation or recession. In hard times shoppers have less to spend and resist high prices.
PRC-01.Brand image: The reputation a brand has with the public. A respected name can charge more than an unknown one for a similar product.
PRC-01.Quality: How well the product is made and performs. Better quality costs more to produce, and customers expect to pay more for it.
PRC-01.Government regulations: Laws that limit how prices may be set, such as bans on price fixing and rules against misleading price claims.
PRC-01.Consumer perceptions: What customers believe a product is worth. Their sense of value sets the highest price they will accept.
PRC-01.Company objectives: What the business wants its pricing to achieve, such as maximum profit, higher market share or a target return.
PRC-01.Target market: The group of customers the business is aiming at. Their income and expectations decide which price levels will work.
PRC-01.Elasticity of demand: How strongly the quantity people buy reacts to a price change. If demand is elastic, a price rise drives many buyers away.
PRC-01.Taxes: Charges set by government, such as sales tax and tariffs on imports, which add to the cost of a product and so to its final price.
PRC-01.Seasonality: Regular changes in demand through the year. Prices often rise in the peak season and are cut when the season ends.
PRC-01.Product life cycle stage: Where the product is in its life, from introduction to decline. Prices often start high or low at launch and fall as it ages.
PRC-01.Substitutes: Other products that can meet the same need. The more substitutes customers can switch to, the less a business can raise its price.
PRC-01.Location: Where the product is sold. Rents, wages, shipping costs and local competition differ from place to place, and so do prices.
PRC-01.Marketing strategy: The overall plan for the product. Price must fit the product, place and promotion, so a luxury position needs a high price.
PRC-01.Channel members: The wholesalers and retailers that handle the product. Each adds its own markup, which raises the final price to the consumer.
PRC-01.Exchange rates: The value of one country's currency against another's. A change makes imported and exported goods cheaper or more expensive.

PRC-02.Maximize profit: Setting the price that leaves the largest gap between total revenue and total costs. Not always the highest price.
PRC-02.Increase sales volume: Pricing to sell as many units or earn as much revenue as possible, often by keeping prices low.
PRC-02.Gain market share: Pricing to win a bigger portion of the industry's total sales, even if profit per item is lower for a while.
PRC-02.Meet the competition: Pricing at about the same level as rivals so the business stays in the game and competes on other things, such as service.
PRC-02.Cover costs: Pricing at least high enough that revenue equals the cost of making and selling the product, so the business breaks even.
PRC-02.Attract customers: Using low or special prices to bring more shoppers into the store or onto the website, where they may buy other things too.
PRC-02.Return on investment: Pricing to earn a chosen percentage of profit on the money the business has put into the product.
PRC-02.Improve image: Using price to shape how people see the product, for example a high price to suggest quality and prestige.
PRC-02.Clear inventory: Lowering prices to sell off old, seasonal or excess stock, which frees up cash and space for new goods.
PRC-02.Enter a new market: Setting a low opening price so a new product or company can win its first customers in a market where it is unknown.
PRC-02.Survival: Pricing just to bring in enough money to keep the business running through a hard period, even with little or no profit.
PRC-02.Improve cash flow: Pricing to bring money in quickly, such as with discounts for fast payment or sales that turn stock into cash.
PRC-02.Build customer loyalty: Pricing fairly and steadily, or rewarding repeat buyers, so that customers keep coming back.
PRC-02.Discourage competitors: Keeping prices low enough that other firms see little profit in entering the market. Pricing meant to destroy rivals can be illegal.
PRC-02.Price stability: Keeping prices steady and in line with rivals to avoid price wars that would cut every firm's profit.
PRC-02.Social responsibility: Setting prices with the public good in mind, such as keeping an essential product affordable for people who need it.

PRC-03.Student discount: A lower price offered to people who can show they are students, a group with little money that may become loyal customers.
PRC-03.Quantity discount: A lower price per unit given to buyers who purchase a large amount, rewarding them for buying in bulk.
PRC-03.Coupon: A printed or digital certificate or code that gives the holder a set amount or percentage off at purchase.
PRC-03.Seasonal discount: A price cut for buying out of season, such as winter coats in spring, which helps sellers even out demand and clear stock.
PRC-03.Employee discount: A reduced price a business gives its own workers on the products it sells, as a benefit of the job.
PRC-03.Senior discount: A lower price offered to older customers, usually those above a set age such as 60 or 65.
PRC-03.Military discount: A reduced price offered to people serving in the armed forces and often to veterans, as a mark of thanks.
PRC-03.Rebate: Money returned to the buyer after the purchase, usually by the manufacturer once proof of purchase is sent in.
PRC-03.Trade-in allowance: A reduction in the price of a new item given in exchange for the buyer's old one, as with cars and phones.
PRC-03.Markdown: A reduction from the original selling price, usually taken by a retailer to sell goods that are moving slowly.
PRC-03.New customer discount: A special price on a first purchase, offered to persuade people to try the business.
PRC-03.Group discount: A lower price per person when a set number of people buy together, as with tickets or tours.
PRC-03.Bundle discount: A saving given when several products are bought together as a package instead of one at a time.
PRC-03.Cash discount: A small price reduction given to a buyer who pays the bill promptly. For example, 2/10 net 30 means 2 percent off if paid within 10 days.
PRC-03.Loyalty discount: A lower price given to repeat customers or members of a rewards program as a thank-you for their continued business.
PRC-03.Early bird discount: A lower price for buying or booking ahead of time or before a deadline, which helps the seller plan and brings money in sooner.
PRC-03.Referral discount: A price reduction or credit given to a customer for bringing in a new customer, and often to the new customer as well.
PRC-03.Teacher discount: A reduced price offered to teachers and other educators, often on books, supplies and technology.
PRC-03.Trade discount: A reduction from the list price that a producer gives wholesalers and retailers to pay them for the selling and storing they do.
PRC-03.Promotional allowance: A payment or price reduction a producer gives a retailer in return for advertising or displaying its product.
PRC-03.Birthday discount: A special offer sent to a customer for their birthday, a personal reward that prompts a visit.
PRC-03.Cumulative quantity discount: A discount based on a buyer's total purchases over a period, such as a year, which encourages repeat buying from one seller.
PRC-03.Slotting allowance: A fee a manufacturer pays a retailer to obtain shelf space for a product, especially a new one.
PRC-03.Freight allowance: A price reduction or payment from the seller that covers all or part of the buyer's cost of shipping the goods.

PRC-04.Price fixing: Competing businesses secretly agreeing on the prices they will charge instead of competing. It is illegal under antitrust law.
PRC-04.Price gouging: Sharply raising the prices of essentials such as water, fuel or generators during an emergency. Many states have laws against it.
PRC-04.Bait and switch: Advertising a low-priced item the seller does not really intend to sell, then pushing shoppers toward a more expensive one.
PRC-04.Price discrimination: Charging competing business buyers different prices for the same goods without a cost reason, which can harm competition.
PRC-04.Predatory pricing: Setting prices very low, often below cost, to drive competitors out of business, intending to raise prices once they are gone.
PRC-04.Deceptive pricing: Misleading customers about a price, such as advertising a discount from a made-up original price.
PRC-04.Hidden fees: Extra charges that are not shown in the advertised price and only appear later, often at checkout. Also called drip pricing.
PRC-04.Bid rigging: Competitors secretly agreeing in advance who will win a contract and what each will bid, so the buyer pays more.
PRC-04.Dumping: Selling goods in a foreign market for less than they sell for at home or less than they cost to make, which can hurt local producers.
PRC-04.Resale price maintenance: A manufacturer requiring retailers to sell its product at or above a set price. Federal courts now judge such agreements case by case, and some states still ban them.
PRC-04.Selling below cost: Pricing goods under what the seller paid for them. Some states have minimum price laws that forbid it, which can limit loss leaders.

PRC-05.Markup: The amount a store adds to what it paid for an item to arrive at its selling price. Selling price minus cost.
PRC-05.Cost: What the store pays its supplier for an item. It is the starting figure to which the markup is added.
PRC-05.Selling price: The amount the customer pays for an item. It equals the item's cost plus the markup. Also called the retail price.
PRC-05.Markdown: The amount by which a store lowers an item's selling price, usually to move slow or leftover stock.
PRC-05.Profit: The money left from sales after all costs and expenses are paid. Markup must cover expenses before any profit remains.
PRC-05.Discount: A reduction from the regular price, given as a dollar amount or as a percentage taken off.
PRC-05.Gross margin: Sales minus the cost of the goods sold, often shown as a percentage of sales. It must cover operating expenses and profit.
PRC-05.Sale price: The lower price an item sells for after a markdown or discount has been taken off the original price.
PRC-05.Original price: The first price a store puts on an item, before any markdowns. The percent off shown on a sale tag is figured from it.
PRC-05.Markup percentage: The markup shown as a percent, found by dividing the dollar markup by either the cost or the selling price.
PRC-05.Markdown percentage: The markdown shown as a percent. For one item, divide the dollar markdown by the original price. Store reports often divide total markdowns by net sales instead.
PRC-05.List price: The price the manufacturer suggests a product should sell for, also called the manufacturer's suggested retail price (MSRP). Discounts are figured from it.
PRC-05.Break-even point: The level of sales at which total revenue exactly equals total costs, so there is neither profit nor loss.
PRC-05.Markup on cost: Markup shown as a percentage of the item's cost. An item that costs $50 and sells for $75 has a 50 percent markup on cost.
PRC-05.Markup on retail: Markup shown as a percentage of the selling price. An item that costs $50 and sells for $75 has a 33.3 percent markup on retail.
PRC-05.Keystone pricing: Setting the selling price at double the cost. The markup is 100 percent of cost, or 50 percent of the retail price.
PRC-05.Initial markup: The difference between an item's cost and the first selling price put on it, before any markdowns are taken.
PRC-05.Maintained markup: The markup a store actually ends up earning, based on the final prices goods really sold for after markdowns.
PRC-05.Additional markup: An increase in an item's price above the original selling price, taken after the goods were first priced and put out for sale.
PRC-05.Markdown cancellation: Raising the price of a marked-down item back toward its original price, for example when a temporary sale ends.

PRC-06.End of season: Seasonal goods, such as winter coats or holiday decorations, are reduced when the season ends because few people will buy them later.
PRC-06.Overstock: The store bought more of an item than it can sell at full price, so it cuts the price to reduce the extra inventory.
PRC-06.Slow sales: An item is not selling as fast as expected, so the price is lowered to give shoppers a stronger reason to buy it.
PRC-06.Match competitor prices: A rival is selling the same item for less, so the store drops its price to avoid losing customers.
PRC-06.Increase sales: A lower price is used to sell more units and bring in more revenue during a slow period.
PRC-06.Damaged goods: Items that are scratched, dented, soiled or in torn packaging are reduced because shoppers will not pay full price for them.
PRC-06.Attract customers: Prices are cut for a sale event to draw shoppers into the store, where they often buy full-priced items as well.
PRC-06.Discontinued item: A product the maker has stopped producing or the store will no longer carry is reduced to sell off the remaining units.
PRC-06.Near expiration: Food and other perishable goods close to their date are reduced so they sell before they must be thrown away.
PRC-06.Make room for new stock: Older merchandise is reduced to empty shelves and storage space for new goods that are about to arrive.
PRC-06.Outdated model: A newer version has come out or styles have changed, so the old one is reduced because fewer people want it.
PRC-06.Buying error: The store's buyer chose the wrong styles, sizes, colors or amounts, and the price is cut to correct the mistake.
PRC-06.Raise cash: The store needs money quickly, for example to pay bills, so it cuts prices to turn inventory into cash.
PRC-06.Going out of business: A store that is closing reduces everything to sell its whole inventory before it shuts. Also called liquidation.
PRC-06.Broken assortment: Only a few odd sizes, colors or pieces of a line are left, so the leftovers are reduced to clear them out.
PRC-06.Pricing error: The original price was set too high for what customers will pay, so the store lowers it to a level that sells.
PRC-06.Floor sample: An item that has been on display or handled by shoppers is reduced because it is no longer in brand-new condition.

CHN-01.Department store: A large store organized into separate sections that sells many kinds of goods, such as clothing, cosmetics and home furnishings.
CHN-01.Supermarket: A large self-service store that sells a wide range of food and household products at fairly low prices.
CHN-01.Online retailer: A business that sells to consumers through a website or app and delivers the goods, instead of using a physical shop.
CHN-01.Convenience store: A small store in a handy location with long opening hours and a limited range of everyday items, usually at higher prices.
CHN-01.Discount store: A store that sells a wide variety of goods at low prices by keeping service and costs down and selling in high volume.
CHN-01.Brick-and-mortar store: A retailer with a physical building that customers visit in person, as opposed to one that sells only online.
CHN-01.Specialty store: A store that carries a narrow range of products with a deep choice within it, such as a shoe store or bookstore.
CHN-01.Warehouse club: A no-frills store that sells goods in bulk at low prices to customers who pay a yearly membership fee.
CHN-01.Outlet store: A store, often owned by the manufacturer, that sells its own surplus, past-season or slightly flawed goods at reduced prices.
CHN-01.Drugstore: A store built around a pharmacy that fills prescriptions and also sells health, beauty and everyday convenience items.
CHN-01.Dollar store: A small discount store selling a mix of inexpensive household goods, many at one very low price point.
CHN-01.Chain store: One of a group of stores under the same ownership and name, selling the same goods with central buying and management.
CHN-01.Supercenter: A very large store that combines a full supermarket with a discount general merchandise store under one roof.
CHN-01.Vending machine: A machine that sells items such as snacks and drinks automatically, with no staff, at any hour.
CHN-01.Pop-up shop: A temporary store opened for a short time, often to test a location, launch a product or sell seasonal goods.
CHN-01.Thrift store: A store that sells used goods at low prices. Many are run by charities and stocked with donated items.
CHN-01.Independent retailer: A store owned and run by one person or family that is not part of a chain, such as a local hardware shop.
CHN-01.Franchise: A store run by a local owner who pays for the right to use a larger company's name, products and operating methods.
CHN-01.Off-price retailer: A store that buys brand-name overruns and leftover stock cheaply and sells them below regular retail prices.
CHN-01.Catalog retailer: A business that sells from a printed or online catalog, taking orders by mail, phone or web and shipping to the customer.
CHN-01.Direct seller: A retailer that sells to consumers in person away from a store, such as door to door or at home parties.
CHN-01.Kiosk: A small open stand or booth, often in a mall walkway or airport, selling a narrow range of goods.
CHN-01.Service retailer: A business whose main offering to consumers is a service instead of a good, such as a salon, restaurant or dry cleaner.
CHN-01.Category killer: A big specialty store with such a huge selection and low prices in one product category that smaller rivals struggle to compete.
CHN-01.Television home shopping: Retailing in which products are shown and described on a television channel and viewers order by phone or online.

CHN-02.Transportation: Physically moving goods from where they are made to where they are sold or used, by truck, rail, ship, air or pipeline.
CHN-02.Warehousing: Storing goods safely until they are needed, in warehouses or in distribution centers that move goods through quickly.
CHN-02.Inventory management: Keeping track of how much stock is on hand and deciding when and how much to reorder, to avoid running out or holding too much.
CHN-02.Order processing: Receiving a customer's order, checking it, picking the goods and preparing them and the paperwork for shipment.
CHN-02.Packaging: Wrapping, boxing or crating goods so they are protected from damage and easy to handle while being stored and shipped.
CHN-02.Materials handling: Moving goods short distances within a warehouse or between vehicles, such as loading and unloading with forklifts and conveyors.
CHN-02.Receiving: Accepting deliveries as they arrive and checking them against the order for the right items, quantities and condition.
CHN-02.Shipment tracking: Following the location and progress of goods while they are in transit, often with barcodes or the Global Positioning System (GPS).
