MKR-11.Buying habits: How, when, where and how often customers shop, and what influences their choices.
MKR-11.Best price: How much customers are willing to pay and how sales would change if the price went up or down.
MKR-11.Market size: How many potential buyers there are and how much they might spend, which shows whether a market is worth entering.
MKR-11.Market trends: The direction in which tastes, technology and spending are moving, so the business can prepare for what customers will want next.
MKR-11.New product ideas: Which new products customers might want and how they react to an idea or sample before the company invests in a full launch.
MKR-11.Advertising effectiveness: Whether advertising reaches the right people, is remembered and leads to sales, and which messages and media work best.
MKR-11.Brand awareness: How many people know the brand and what they think of it compared with competing brands.
MKR-11.Best location: Where a store or branch would draw enough customers, judged by nearby population, traffic, income levels and competitors.
MKR-11.Product improvements: What customers dislike or find missing in a current product, so the company knows what to fix or add.
MKR-11.Market share: The portion of total sales in a market that the company holds compared with its competitors.
MKR-11.Sales forecast: An estimate of how much the business is likely to sell in a future period, used to plan production, staffing and budgets.
MKR-11.Market opportunities: Customer needs that no one is serving well, or new groups and places where the business could sell.
MKR-11.Economic conditions: How factors such as employment, inflation and consumer confidence are affecting what customers can and will spend.
MKR-11.Customer loyalty: How likely customers are to buy again and to recommend the business to others, instead of switching to a rival.
MKR-11.Reasons for lost sales: Why sales are dropping or why former customers stopped buying, so the cause of the problem can be corrected.
MKR-11.Best distribution channels: Where and how customers prefer to buy, such as in stores, online or through dealers, so the product is sold in the right places.
MKR-11.Packaging preferences: Which package designs, sizes and labels shoppers notice, understand and prefer.

PROM-08.Increase sales: Getting more units sold or more revenue in a set period, the most common and most easily measured promotional goal.
PROM-08.Build awareness: Making more people in the target market know that the brand or product exists. It is the first step toward any sale.
PROM-08.Inform customers: Telling people what a product is, what it does, what it costs and where to get it, which matters most for new or complex products.
PROM-08.Persuade customers: Convincing people to prefer the product over competing ones and to buy it, by stressing its benefits.
PROM-08.Attract new customers: Reaching people who have never bought from the business and giving them a reason to make a first purchase.
PROM-08.Remind customers: Keeping a well-known product in people's minds so they think of it when they are next ready to buy.
PROM-08.Introduce a new product: Announcing a launch so the market learns what the new product is, how it helps them and where it is sold.
PROM-08.Improve company image: Building goodwill and a positive reputation for the business as a whole, not selling one particular item.
PROM-08.Increase store traffic: Bringing more shoppers into a store or onto a website, where they may buy the promoted item and other things as well.
PROM-08.Build customer loyalty: Encouraging current customers to keep buying and to choose the brand again, instead of switching to a competitor.
PROM-08.Encourage trial: Getting people to try a product for the first time, often through samples, coupons or introductory offers.
PROM-08.Increase market share: Winning a larger portion of the total sales in the market, which means taking customers from competitors.
PROM-08.Stimulate demand: Raising interest in a product so more people want it, sometimes for a whole product category and not just one brand.
PROM-08.Differentiate the product: Showing how the product is different from and better than competing products, so it holds a clear place in customers' minds.
PROM-08.Generate leads: Collecting names and contact details of people who show interest, so that salespeople can follow up with them.
PROM-08.Respond to competitors: Answering a rival's advertising or special offers so that customers are not drawn away.
PROM-08.Clear inventory: Selling off extra, seasonal or older stock quickly to free up cash and space for new merchandise.
PROM-08.Stabilize sales: Evening out the highs and lows in sales, for example by promoting a seasonal product during its slow months.
PROM-08.Support the sales force: Making the selling job easier by building interest and supplying leads before a salesperson contacts the customer.
PROM-08.Gain channel support: Persuading wholesalers and retailers to stock, display and push the product. Promotion aimed at them is part of a push strategy.
PROM-08.Correct misinformation: Fixing a false impression or answering bad publicity, so that customers have accurate facts about the company or product.

PROM-09.Humor: Making the audience laugh so the ad is noticed, liked and remembered. The risk is that people recall the joke but not the brand.
PROM-09.Celebrity endorsement: A famous person uses or recommends the product, so that fans transfer their liking and trust for the star to the brand.
PROM-09.Emotional appeal: An appeal aimed at feelings such as love, joy, pride or belonging instead of at facts and logic.
PROM-09.Fear appeal: Showing a danger or loss the audience wants to avoid, then offering the product as protection, as in ads for insurance or alarm systems.
PROM-09.Bandwagon: Suggesting that everyone is buying the product, so the viewer should join in and not be left out.
PROM-09.Testimonial: An ordinary customer describes a good experience with the product, which seems more believable than the company praising itself.
PROM-09.Sex appeal: Using attractive people or romance to draw attention and suggest the product will make the buyer more appealing.
PROM-09.Rational appeal: An appeal to logic and self-interest that gives facts, figures and practical reasons, such as quality, performance or savings.
PROM-09.Price appeal: Stressing a low price, a sale or good value for money as the main reason to buy.
PROM-09.Scarcity: Stressing that the offer ends soon or that supplies are limited, which pushes people to act now instead of waiting.
PROM-09.Music: Using a jingle or a well-known song so the message is pleasant to hear and stays in the listener's memory.
PROM-09.Nostalgia: Stirring warm memories of the past so that those good feelings attach to the brand.
PROM-09.Expert endorsement: A doctor, engineer or other authority backs the product, or test results are cited, to make its claims more believable.
PROM-09.Demonstration: Showing the product working, often before and after or under tough conditions, so viewers see the proof for themselves.
PROM-09.Slice of life: A short scene of ordinary people in an everyday situation in which the product solves a common problem.
PROM-09.Snob appeal: Suggesting that the product is for a select, superior few and that owning it will raise the buyer's status.
PROM-09.Plain folks: Presenting the product as the choice of ordinary, down-to-earth people just like the audience.
PROM-09.Patriotism: Linking the product to love of country, for example by stressing that it is made at home or supports national pride.
PROM-09.Health appeal: Promising that the product will help the buyer stay well, fit or safe, as in ads for foods, vitamins and exercise equipment.
PROM-09.Comparison: Showing the product against a competing product to claim it is better on a point such as price, taste or performance.
PROM-09.Repetition: Repeating a name, slogan or message many times so that it sticks in memory.
PROM-09.Lifestyle: Showing how the product fits a way of living the audience has or wants, such as an active, outdoor life.
PROM-09.Guilt: Making the audience feel they ought to act, for example to protect their family or help a cause, and offering the product as the way to do it.
PROM-09.Glittering generalities: Using vague, pleasant words such as best, natural or amazing that sound impressive but promise nothing specific.
PROM-09.Adventure: Linking the product with excitement, risk and exploration, as in many ads for trucks, sports drinks and outdoor gear.
PROM-09.Transfer: Placing the product next to something people already admire, such as a flag, a hero or a beautiful scene, so the good feeling carries over.
PROM-09.Fantasy: Building a dreamlike or imaginary world around the product, a style often used for perfume and luxury goods.

PROM-10.Social media marketing: Using platforms where people share and follow content to post about a brand, run paid ads and talk with customers.
PROM-10.Email marketing: Sending newsletters, offers and reminders to people who have given the business their email address.
PROM-10.Search engine optimization: Improving a website's content and structure so it appears higher in unpaid search results. Known as SEO.
PROM-10.Influencer marketing: Paying or partnering with people who have a large or loyal online following to show and recommend a product to their audience.
PROM-10.Website: The business's own home online, where visitors learn about products, buy, sign up or make contact. Most other digital tactics send people here.
PROM-10.Pay-per-click advertising: Online ads, often shown beside search results, for which the advertiser pays only when someone clicks. Known as PPC.
PROM-10.Content marketing: Publishing useful or entertaining material, such as blog posts, guides and how-to videos, to attract an audience and earn its trust.
PROM-10.Video marketing: Promoting a product with online video, from short clips and tutorials to live streams and paid video ads.
PROM-10.Display advertising: Image or banner ads placed on websites and apps that people visit, usually bought through ad networks.
PROM-10.Mobile marketing: Reaching people on their phones through text messages, app notifications and ads designed for small screens.
PROM-10.Affiliate marketing: Paying other websites or creators a commission for each sale or lead they send through a special tracking link.
PROM-10.Online reviews: Encouraging customers to post ratings and comments and replying to them, because shoppers read reviews before they buy.
PROM-10.Retargeting: Showing ads to people who have already visited a website or looked at a product, to bring them back to finish the purchase.
PROM-10.Podcast: Sponsoring or advertising on audio shows that listeners follow, or producing a show to build an audience for the brand.
PROM-10.Webinars: Live or recorded online seminars that teach something useful and collect the contact details of the people who sign up.
PROM-10.Viral marketing: Creating content that people want to share, so the message spreads quickly from person to person at little cost.
PROM-10.Local search listings: Keeping a business's name, address, hours and photos accurate on search and map services so nearby customers can find it.
PROM-10.Marketing automation: Software that sends messages automatically when a customer takes an action, such as a welcome email after signing up.
PROM-10.Native advertising: Paid content designed to look like the articles or posts around it and labeled as sponsored.
PROM-10.Chatbots: Chat windows on a website or app, often run by automated programs, that answer visitors' questions at any hour and guide them toward a purchase.
PROM-10.User-generated content: Photos, videos and posts about a brand made by its customers, which the brand encourages and shares because people trust other buyers.
PROM-10.Location-based marketing: Sending offers or ads to people's phones based on where they are, such as when they come near a store.

PROM-11.Reach: The number or percentage of different people in the target audience who are exposed to an ad at least once during a set period.
PROM-11.Frequency: The average number of times a person in the audience is exposed to the ad during a set period.
PROM-11.Impressions: The total number of times an ad is seen or heard, counting every exposure, even when the same person sees it more than once.
PROM-11.Prime time: The evening hours when television audiences are largest, which makes commercial time then the most expensive.
PROM-11.Target audience: The specific group of people a campaign is meant to reach. Media are chosen by how well their audiences match this group.
PROM-11.Circulation: The number of copies of a newspaper or magazine that are sold or distributed, used to judge its reach and to set ad prices.
PROM-11.Cost per thousand: The cost of reaching one thousand people or impressions with an ad, known as CPM. It lets a planner compare media of different sizes.
PROM-11.Ratings: The percentage of all households or people in a market tuned to a program. One rating point equals one percent of that population.
PROM-11.Media mix: The combination of media, such as television, radio, print and online, that a campaign uses to deliver its message.
PROM-11.Media schedule: The plan showing exactly when and where each ad will run over the life of the campaign.
PROM-11.Lead time: How far ahead of the run date a medium needs the finished ad. Magazines need weeks or months, while radio and online need far less.
PROM-11.Rate card: A list published by a media company showing what it charges for ad space or time, along with sizes, deadlines and discounts.
PROM-11.Ad spot: One slot of commercial time on radio or television, usually sold in set lengths such as 15, 30 or 60 seconds.
PROM-11.Drive time: The morning and late-afternoon commuting hours, when radio audiences are largest and airtime costs the most.
PROM-11.Gross rating points: A measure of a campaign's total weight, found by multiplying reach, as a percentage, by average frequency. Known as GRPs.
PROM-11.Share: The percentage of households with sets in use at that moment that are tuned to a particular program.
PROM-11.Readership: The total number of people who read a publication, which is larger than its circulation because one copy is often read by several people.
PROM-11.Continuity: A scheduling pattern in which ads run at a steady level throughout the campaign period, with no breaks.
PROM-11.Clutter: The crowd of competing ads surrounding a message in a medium. The more clutter there is, the harder it is for one ad to be noticed.
PROM-11.Media vehicle: One specific carrier within a medium, such as a particular magazine title, television program or website.
PROM-11.Daypart: One of the blocks of time into which a broadcast day is divided for selling ads, such as morning, daytime and late night.
PROM-11.Flighting: A scheduling pattern that alternates periods of advertising with periods of none, often matched to seasonal demand.
PROM-11.Pulsing: A scheduling pattern that keeps a low level of advertising running all the time and adds heavier bursts at key periods.
PROM-11.Cost per point: The cost of buying one rating point in a market, used to compare the price of programs or stations.
PROM-11.Share of voice: A brand's advertising as a percentage of all advertising in its product category, a measure of how loud it is next to rivals.
PROM-11.Column inch: A unit for selling newspaper ad space: one column wide by one inch deep.
PROM-11.Waste coverage: The part of a medium's audience that falls outside the advertiser's target market, so money spent reaching it brings no return.

SEL-09.Good listener: Paying full attention to what the customer says, and asking questions, in order to learn what the customer really needs.
SEL-09.Communication skills: Explaining ideas clearly in speech and writing and getting along well with many kinds of people.
SEL-09.Product knowledge: Knowing the product's features, benefits, uses and limits well enough to answer questions and recommend the right item.
SEL-09.Confidence: Believing in oneself and the product, which helps a salesperson speak with assurance and ask for the sale.
SEL-09.Friendliness: A warm, pleasant manner that puts customers at ease and makes them willing to talk about what they need.
SEL-09.Persistence: Continuing to try after hearing no. Many sales are closed only after several contacts with the same prospect.
SEL-09.Honesty: Telling the truth about what a product can and cannot do. Trust is what brings customers back and earns referrals.
SEL-09.Enthusiasm: Real energy and excitement about the product, which customers notice and often come to share.
SEL-09.Empathy: The ability to see a situation from the customer's side and understand the customer's feelings and concerns.
SEL-09.Persuasiveness: The ability to present benefits and answer doubts so that the customer becomes convinced the product is right.
SEL-09.Self-motivation: Working hard toward goals without being pushed. It matters in sales because many salespeople work alone and are paid by results.
SEL-09.Patience: Staying calm and giving customers the time they need to ask questions and decide, without pressuring them.
SEL-09.Organization: Planning time, calls, appointments and paperwork well, so that no customer or follow-up is forgotten.
SEL-09.Problem solving: Working out how a product or a mix of products can fix the customer's particular problem.
SEL-09.Creativity: Finding fresh ways to reach prospects, present a product or put together an offer when the usual approach does not work.
SEL-09.Relationship building: Earning a customer's trust over time so that the customer keeps buying and recommends the salesperson to others.
SEL-09.Professional appearance: Dressing and grooming in a way that fits the job and makes a good first impression on customers.
SEL-09.Adaptability: Changing the sales approach to suit each customer and situation instead of giving everyone the same presentation.
SEL-09.Negotiation skills: Reaching agreement on price and terms in a way that satisfies both the customer and the company.
SEL-09.Dependability: Doing what was promised, on time, such as returning calls and checking that an order arrived correctly.
SEL-09.Tact: Saying the right thing in the right way, so that a customer is not embarrassed or offended even when being corrected.
SEL-09.Coachability: Being willing to accept feedback from managers and to keep learning new products and better selling methods.
SEL-09.Observation skills: Noticing a customer's body language, tone and reactions, which signal interest, doubt or readiness to buy.

SEL-10.Commission: Pay based on results, usually a percentage of each sale. Under straight commission a salesperson who sells nothing earns nothing. A graduated plan raises the rate as sales grow.
SEL-10.Salary: A fixed amount of pay, by the year or by the hour, whatever the sales level. It gives security but less incentive to sell more.
SEL-10.Bonus: An extra payment for reaching or beating a target, such as a quarterly sales goal.
SEL-10.Salary plus commission: A combination plan: a fixed base salary for security with commission on top as a reward for selling more.
SEL-10.Sales contests: Short competitions among salespeople, with prizes for those who sell the most or reach a set goal.
SEL-10.Recognition: Public praise, awards and titles for top performers, which motivate through pride and status instead of money.
SEL-10.Sales quotas: Sales targets set for each salesperson for a period. They give a clear goal, and pay or bonuses are often tied to reaching them.
SEL-10.Incentive trips: Travel paid for by the company as a reward for salespeople who reach a high target.
SEL-10.Promotions: Moving strong performers up to better positions, such as senior salesperson or sales manager.
SEL-10.Company car: A vehicle, or money toward one, provided to salespeople who must travel to call on customers.
SEL-10.Expense account: Money from the company to cover the costs of selling, such as travel, hotels and meals with clients.
SEL-10.Benefits: Compensation other than direct pay, such as health insurance, paid vacation and a retirement plan.
SEL-10.Training: Teaching and coaching that build product knowledge and selling skills, which raise both confidence and results.
SEL-10.Profit sharing: Paying employees a share of the company's profits, so salespeople gain when the whole business does well.
SEL-10.Stock options: The right to buy company shares at a set price, which rewards salespeople when the company's value rises.
SEL-10.Merchandise rewards: Goods or gift cards given as prizes for reaching sales goals, in place of cash.
SEL-10.Draw against commission: An advance paid to a salesperson and later subtracted from the commissions earned, which evens out income in slow periods.
SEL-10.Push money: A small payment, also called a spiff, that a manufacturer or store gives salespeople for each unit of a particular product they sell.
SEL-10.Sales meetings: Gatherings where salespeople learn about new products, share ideas, are recognized and are encouraged toward new goals.
SEL-10.Presidents club: An honor group for the top salespeople of the year, who usually receive special recognition and a reward trip.

SEL-11.Consultative selling: The salesperson acts as an expert adviser, asking questions to understand the customer's situation before recommending anything.
SEL-11.Hard sell: An aggressive, high-pressure style that pushes the customer to buy right away. It can win a sale but often costs repeat business.
SEL-11.Canned presentation: A memorized or scripted presentation given the same way to every customer. It is consistent and easy to train but cannot adjust to the buyer. Also called stimulus-response selling.
SEL-11.Relationship selling: Selling that aims to build a long-term bond of trust with the customer, valuing future business above any single sale.
SEL-11.Demonstration: Showing the product in action, and often letting the customer handle it, so the benefits are seen instead of just described.
SEL-11.Solution selling: The salesperson first uncovers the customer's problem, then presents a product or package of products as the answer to it.
SEL-11.Soft sell: A relaxed, low-pressure style that informs and suggests and lets the customer decide without being pushed.
SEL-11.Feature-benefit selling: Matching each product feature to what it does for the customer, so the buyer hears benefits and not just technical facts.
SEL-11.Need-satisfaction presentation: A flexible presentation in which the salesperson asks questions and listens first, then shows how the product meets the needs uncovered.
SEL-11.Team selling: Several people from the selling company, such as a salesperson, an engineer and a finance specialist, work together on one customer.
SEL-11.Suggestion selling: Recommending related items, a larger size or a better model that would add to the customer's original purchase.
SEL-11.Formula presentation: A presentation that follows a set series of steps, most often gaining attention, then interest, then desire, then action (AIDA).
SEL-11.SPIN selling: A questioning method built on four kinds of questions: situation, problem, implication and need-payoff.
SEL-11.Social selling: Using social media to find prospects, share useful content and build relationships that lead to sales conversations.
SEL-11.Transactional selling: Selling that focuses on completing a quick, single sale, usually on price, with little effort to build a lasting relationship.
SEL-11.Value selling: Showing in measurable terms, such as money saved or earned, what the product is worth to the customer, instead of competing on price.
SEL-11.Virtual selling: Presenting to customers at a distance through video calls, screen sharing and online demonstrations instead of meeting in person.
SEL-11.Challenger selling: An approach in which the salesperson teaches the customer something new about the customer's own business and challenges the customer's assumptions.
SEL-11.Adaptive selling: Changing the presentation during the sales call to fit the customer's personality, needs and reactions.
SEL-11.Partnership selling: Working with a customer as a long-term partner, with both companies planning together so that each one gains.

MKT-12.Marketing manager: The person who plans and directs a company's marketing: choosing target markets and overseeing products, pricing, promotion and the marketing budget.
MKT-12.Social media manager: The person who plans and posts a brand's content on social platforms, replies to followers and tracks how the posts perform.
MKT-12.Graphic designer: A person who creates the visual side of marketing, such as logos, packaging, advertisements and web pages.
MKT-12.Salesperson: A person who deals directly with customers, finds out what they need, presents products and closes sales.
MKT-12.Market research analyst: A person who collects and studies data about customers, competitors and markets and reports what it means for marketing decisions.
MKT-12.Copywriter: A person who writes the words of advertisements, such as headlines, slogans, scripts and web text.
MKT-12.Brand manager: The person responsible for one brand or product line, including its image, pricing, promotion and profit.
MKT-12.Public relations specialist: A person who manages an organization's public image by writing news releases, working with reporters and handling bad publicity.
MKT-12.Advertising manager: The person who plans a company's advertising, sets the budget, works with ad agencies and approves campaigns.
MKT-12.Digital marketing specialist: A person who runs online marketing, such as email campaigns, search and social media ads, and the company website.
MKT-12.Account executive: At an advertising agency, the person who manages the relationship with a client and coordinates the agency's work for that client.
MKT-12.Influencer: A person with an online following who is paid, or given products, by brands to show and recommend them to that audience.
MKT-12.Chief marketing officer: The top marketing executive in a company, known as the CMO, who sets overall marketing strategy and reports to the chief executive.
MKT-12.Art director: The person who decides how an advertisement looks, choosing its layout, images, colors and type, usually working alongside a copywriter.
MKT-12.Creative director: The person who leads an agency's or company's creative team and approves the ideas, writing and design of its campaigns.
MKT-12.Media buyer: A person who negotiates for and purchases advertising time and space, aiming to reach the target audience at the lowest cost.
MKT-12.Event planner: A person who organizes promotional events such as product launches, trade show exhibits and sponsored activities.
MKT-12.Marketing coordinator: An entry-level position that supports the marketing team by scheduling campaigns, preparing materials and tracking results.
MKT-12.SEO specialist: A person who improves a website so it ranks higher in search results. SEO stands for search engine optimization.
MKT-12.Content marketer: A person who plans and writes articles, videos, guides and posts that attract and inform potential customers.
MKT-12.Retail buyer: A person who chooses and purchases the merchandise a store will sell, judging what customers will want and negotiating with suppliers.
MKT-12.Visual merchandiser: A person who designs store displays, windows and product arrangements so that merchandise attracts shoppers.
MKT-12.Marketing consultant: An outside expert that businesses hire for advice on strategy, branding or campaigns.
MKT-12.Web designer: A person who plans the look and layout of websites so they are attractive, easy to use and good at turning visitors into customers.
MKT-12.Commercial photographer: A person who takes the product, fashion and lifestyle pictures used in advertisements, catalogs and websites.
MKT-12.Pricing analyst: A person who studies costs, competitors and customer demand in order to recommend the prices a company should charge.
MKT-12.Account planner: At an advertising agency, the person who studies the consumer and makes sure the campaign strategy is built on real customer insight.

MKT-13.Lower the price: Cutting the price to attract price-sensitive buyers and to win customers from competitors, usually at the cost of a smaller profit on each unit.
MKT-13.Increase advertising: Running a new or heavier campaign to remind customers of the product, bring back lapsed buyers and defend it against rivals.
MKT-13.Improve the product: Raising quality or adding features so the product feels new again and gives current owners a reason to buy the updated version.
MKT-13.New packaging: Giving the product a fresh package design, size or container so it looks up to date and stands out again on the shelf.
MKT-13.Find new markets: Selling the product to groups that have not bought it before, such as another age group, business buyers or customers in other countries.
MKT-13.Sales promotions: Short-term offers such as coupons, rebates, contests and samples that give shoppers a reason to buy now.
MKT-13.Find new uses: Showing customers other things the product can do. Baking soda sales grew when it was promoted for removing odors as well as for baking.
MKT-13.Line extensions: Adding new flavors, sizes, colors or models under the same brand name to renew interest and reach buyers with different tastes.
MKT-13.Redesign the product: Changing how the product looks or feels, without changing what it does, so it seems modern. Carmakers restyle their models for this reason.
MKT-13.Reposition the product: Changing the image the product holds in customers' minds, for example presenting an everyday item as a healthy or premium choice.
MKT-13.Expand distribution: Making the product available in more places, such as new kinds of stores, online sellers or vending machines.
MKT-13.Rebrand: Giving the product a new name, logo or overall look to shake off a tired image.
MKT-13.Encourage more frequent use: Persuading current customers to use the product more often or in larger amounts, so the same buyers purchase more.
MKT-13.Bundle with other products: Selling the product together with related items at one price, which adds value and moves more units.
MKT-13.Add services: Offering extras around the product, such as a longer warranty, delivery or better support, to set it apart from similar rivals.

MKT-14.Federal Trade Commission Act: The law that created the Federal Trade Commission (FTC) and bans unfair methods of competition and unfair or deceptive business practices.
MKT-14.Sherman Antitrust Act: The first major federal antitrust law. It outlaws agreements that restrain trade, such as price fixing among competitors, and attempts to monopolize a market.
MKT-14.Clayton Act: An antitrust law that adds to the Sherman Act by restricting specific practices, such as tying agreements and mergers, when they would seriously reduce competition.
MKT-14.Consumer Product Safety Act: The law that created the Consumer Product Safety Commission, which sets safety standards for consumer products and can order recalls of dangerous ones.
MKT-14.Robinson-Patman Act: A law that limits price discrimination. A seller generally may not charge competing business buyers different prices for the same goods if doing so harms competition.
MKT-14.CAN-SPAM Act: A law setting rules for commercial email. Messages must not have misleading subject lines and must give recipients a working way to opt out.
MKT-14.Childrens Online Privacy Protection Act: A law, known as COPPA, requiring websites and apps aimed at young children to get a parent's consent before collecting a child's personal information.
MKT-14.Fair Packaging and Labeling Act: A law requiring consumer product labels to state what the product is, who made or distributed it, and the net quantity of the contents.
MKT-14.Federal Food, Drug, and Cosmetic Act: The law that gives the Food and Drug Administration authority over the safety and labeling of food, drugs, medical devices and cosmetics.
MKT-14.Lanham Act: The federal trademark law. It provides for registering and protecting trademarks and lets businesses sue over false advertising.
MKT-14.Nutrition Labeling and Education Act: A law requiring most packaged foods to carry nutrition labeling and setting rules for health and nutrient claims such as low fat.
MKT-14.Magnuson-Moss Warranty Act: A law governing written warranties on consumer products. Warranty terms must be stated clearly and labeled as either full or limited.
MKT-14.Pure Food and Drug Act: An early consumer protection law that banned the sale of mislabeled or contaminated food and medicine across state lines. Today's food and drug law grew out of it.
MKT-14.Truth in Lending Act: A law requiring lenders to disclose the cost and terms of credit clearly, including in advertising, so that borrowers can compare offers.
MKT-14.Wheeler-Lea Act: An amendment to the Federal Trade Commission Act that lets the FTC act against deceptive practices and false advertising that harm consumers, not only competitors.
MKT-14.Telephone Consumer Protection Act: A law restricting telemarketing calls, including calls made with automatic dialers or recorded messages, and unsolicited advertising faxes.
MKT-14.Do-Not-Call Implementation Act: A law that authorized the FTC to collect fees to set up and enforce the National Do Not Call Registry, a list of phone numbers most telemarketers may not call.
MKT-14.Federal Cigarette Labeling and Advertisi: A law requiring health warnings on cigarette packages and in cigarette advertising.
MKT-14.Telemarketing and Consumer Fraud and Abu: A law directing the FTC to write rules against deceptive and abusive telemarketing. The result is known as the Telemarketing Sales Rule.
MKT-14.Consumer Goods Pricing Act: A law that ended federal support for state fair trade laws, which had allowed manufacturers to set minimum retail prices for their products.
MKT-14.Child Protection and Toy Safety Act: A law that allows toys and other children's articles to be banned if they present electrical, mechanical or heat hazards.
MKT-14.Flammable Fabrics Act: A law that sets flammability standards for clothing and household textiles, so that dangerously flammable items cannot be sold.
MKT-14.Poison Prevention Packaging Act: A law requiring child-resistant packaging for dangerous household products and many medicines.
MKT-14.Textile Fiber Products Identification Ac: A law requiring labels on clothing and other textile goods to show the fiber content, the country of origin and the company responsible.
MKT-14.Automobile Information Disclosure Act: A law requiring a window sticker on every new car showing the manufacturer's suggested retail price and the equipment included.
